title: Overlap Rings
description: Fill two rings and look at what falls in both, then settle a multiple with one division instead of two whole lists.
modes: none. One flow, one phase at a time. The host mounts a phase (phase prop). With navigableDots true, or no phase, the child may jump phases with the dots (user mode); otherwise the dots show progress and the teacher agent drives window.toolApi (AI mode). The last phase, and a whole lesson, end on the summary page, where Free play and Play again sit.

writeup.why: Find what two numbers have in common, and learn the single division that settles a multiple without writing any list at all.
writeup.look: Two rings of cord overlapping, filled with lists that stop or with tracks that do not, and a divide gate standing beside them.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Overlap Rings' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the cards lifted into the shared middle against the cards there are to test, two numbers in ink, the first climbing by one as each card crosses and the second fixed at however many cards this phase laid out. In multiple mode the second number is replaced by an open dash rather than by a total, because that list has no length. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The two rings are drawn cord, each 470 across, centred at 420,430 and 700,430 so that they overlap through the middle of the working area, with the chosen number written on the outer edge of each. A third ring of the same size opens below and between them, centred at 560,600, when a third number is added, and the three overlaps are drawn rather than implied. In factor mode each ring fills with its number's factors as cards 84 by 84 laid in order between a wall at one and a wall at the number itself, so each list is visibly shut at both ends, and a card belonging to both lists travels into the overlap and takes the shared colour. In multiple mode the rings straighten into two parallel tracks, each 1086 by 8 at 64,352 and 64,472, running out through the right hand edge of the frame with no end mark and no last step drawn, and the overlap becomes a band 1086 by 112 at 64,368 that keeps catching new numbers as the tracks are run further and never closes. The divide gate stands at the right of the working area, 300 by 400 at 786,202: a bigger number and a smaller one are dropped into its mouth, the division is drawn on a ruled board as that many equal rows separated by walls, and whatever will not fit is set on the leftover shelf, 300 by 76 at 786,618, OUTSIDE the rows on the same surface at full strength and fully countable, never faded and never tucked under a row. Say both then writes the two statements that single division settled, the factor one and the multiple one, inside one frame under the shelf. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across wherever a common factor, a common multiple or a remainder is asked for, and on the second and fourth phases a word pad reading common, both, finite, infinite, factor and multiple, so that a shared list can be described as well as listed. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own: a number that divides another exactly is deep blue, a number built by multiplying is green, anything standing in both lists at once is rose, whatever is left over and any trial that fails is vermilion, the number being broken up or the total in hand is amber, and a single digit being read or added is sky blue. Chrome never borrows one of those and none of them is ever used for chrome, and every reading survives with the colour taken away, because a leftover is told by standing outside the rows before it is told by a band, and a list that stops is told by the wall at each end of it and a list that does not by the open edge of the frame. The two modes are never on the stage at once except where a phase asks for them to be, and when they are, the shut walls of the factor lists and the open edge of the tracks are drawn in the same frame at the same size. That single picture is the whole topic, and two written lists on a page cannot hold it.
writeup.finish: The card shows the last pair the child compared, both rings filled, the overlap still holding what they shared, and the gate's division beside it.

phases.win: the overlap holds exactly the common factors and each one divides both numbers
phases.does: fills each ring and moves whatever belongs to both into the overlap
phases.goal: a common factor is a number standing in both factor lists
phases.says: Fill both rings. Which numbers ended up standing in the middle?
phases.check: Find the common factors of 16 and 18, and say which of them you could have named before starting.
phases.feels: the middle holds only what stood in both lists, and one is always standing in it
phases.hands: Lay two loops of string on the floor so that they overlap, and write twenty-four on one and thirty-two on the other. Hand out number cards from one upward and let each child work out where their card belongs, in one loop, in the other, in the middle, or outside both. Before anybody names the middle, ask what every card lying in it has in common, and ask whether the middle could ever be left empty.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: does that card divide the first number exactly? Second rung, the phase's: does it divide the other one as well? Third rung: the rings are cut to two small numbers and the child fills both and lifts the shared cards across by hand. The number pad stays open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: common sounds like putting the two lists together, and a middle full of cards looks like more of an answer than a middle holding four.
wrong.move: sweeps every factor of both numbers into the middle, so the overlap holds the two lists joined together.
wrong.screen: each card is picked up again and tested against both numbers as it crosses, the division for each drawn on the ruled board beside the rings with its leftover shelf showing. A card that divides only one of the two is set back into that ring rather than removed from the stage, and the middle is read out again once every card has been tested.

wrong.why: a number that turns up in every list anybody ever writes stops looking like a finding, and a child hunting for something interesting will step over it.
wrong.move: leaves one out of the middle because it goes into everything and so does not feel like an answer.
wrong.screen: one is dropped through the gate twice, twenty-four divided by one and thirty-two divided by one, each drawn on the board as a single row with the leftover shelf beside it empty. The card then travels into the middle and takes the shared colour like any other, and the middle is counted out with it in.

phases.screen: two empty rings with both factor lists waiting to be filled
phases.soWhat: A common factor divides both numbers, and one is a common factor of every pair of numbers.

phases.win: the band keeps catching numbers as the tracks run and no last meeting is drawn
phases.does: runs both tracks on and watches the shared band catch new numbers
phases.goal: two lists of multiples keep meeting, so the shared list has no end
phases.says: Keep both tracks running. Do they stop meeting? Could they?
phases.check: Write the first four common multiples of 6 and 8. Is there a greatest one? Say why.
phases.feels: one overlap kept filling and the other one shut
phases.hands: Write the multiples of two along one strip of paper and the multiples of three along another, and lay the two strips one above the other so that the numbers line up. Ring every number that appears on both. When the strips run out, stick more paper on the end of each and carry on, and ask whether the ringing is ever going to stop. Then write the factors of two and the factors of three underneath and ask the same question about those.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which numbers are standing in the band so far? Second rung, the phase's: what happens if both tracks take one more step? Third rung: the tracks are cut to two small step sizes and the child runs them until the band catches something twice. The word pad stays open.

wrong.why: that is where the two written lists stopped, and a list that has stopped looks exactly like a list that has finished.
wrong.move: writes six, twelve and eighteen and reports that those are all the common multiples there are.
wrong.screen: both tracks are run on past the end of the child's lists, one step at a time, and the band catches twenty-four, then thirty, then thirty-six, each meeting drawn as two flags sliding together. The three numbers the child wrote keep their own cards in the band, and the tracks and the band all leave the frame at the right with no end mark drawn on any of them.

wrong.why: both words carry common and both lists were built the same way, so a fact about one of them sounds like a fact about the pair of them.
wrong.move: carries the answer back the other way and says the common factors must be infinite too, since the common multiples are.
wrong.screen: the rings switch to factor mode on the very same two numbers. Two and three fill with their own factors, one and two in the first and one and three in the second, each penned between a wall at one and a wall at the number, and exactly one card travels into the overlap and the middle shuts. The multiple band is left running underneath it at the same time, so the shut middle and the open one are on the stage together.

phases.screen: the rings turned into two tracks leaving the frame with no end drawn
phases.soWhat: Common multiples never run out, because both of the lists they come from never run out.

phases.win: the gate returns an exact answer and the rings stay unused beside it
phases.does: runs the single division and reads the answer with nothing left over
phases.goal: one division settles whether a bigger number is a multiple of a smaller one
phases.says: Must you write both lists to find out? Try one division instead.
phases.check: Is 90 a multiple of 13? Settle it with one division and say what the division showed.
phases.feels: one division, and no list at all
phases.hands: Ask whether a hundred and eight is a multiple of nine, and start writing the multiples of nine on the board deliberately slowly, one line at a time. Partway through, stop and ask whether there is a faster way. Take the answer, do the single division beside the half written list, and leave both on the board together. Then hand out four pairs and let the class settle each one with one division.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which of the two numbers is the bigger one? Second rung, the phase's: what is left when you divide it by the other? Third rung: the gate is cut to two small numbers and the child runs the division and reads the shelf. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: the lists are what the topic has been about for two sessions, and a question about multiples looks like a question that wants a list.
wrong.move: writes out the whole list of multiples of nine looking for a hundred and eight somewhere in it.
wrong.screen: the gate runs its single division on the ruled board beside the list the child is building, twelve rows of nine with nothing on the leftover shelf, and it has finished by the time the fourth line of the list is written. The child's list is left standing and is carried on to the twelfth line afterwards, so that both routes reach the same place and only one of them is short.

wrong.why: the question names the smaller number first and it is the number the child is thinking about, so it arrives at the front of the division.
wrong.move: divides the smaller number by the bigger one, because the smaller number is the one being asked about.
wrong.screen: the gate lays both ways round on the board one above the other. The smaller number divided by the bigger one puts no complete row on the board at all and sets the whole of it on the leftover shelf; the bigger divided by the smaller draws twelve equal rows with the shelf empty. Both boards stay drawn and nothing is marked.

phases.screen: the divide gate loaded with a bigger and a smaller number and the rings dimmed
phases.soWhat: To find out whether a bigger number is a multiple of a smaller one, divide the bigger by the smaller.
phases.concept: One division instead of two lists

phases.win: the leftover stands outside the rows and both statements are written under it
phases.does: counts what is left over and writes both statements the division settled
phases.goal: anything left over settles the factor question and the multiple question at once
phases.says: Something is left over. Say the two things that tells you.
phases.check: Divide 38 by 6, then write the two things that one division has settled.
phases.feels: the leftover answered two questions at once
phases.hands: Put fifty-five counters on the table and share them into seven equal rows. Push whatever will not fit into the middle where everybody can see it and count it out loud. Then ask two questions about that one pile: is fifty-five a multiple of seven, and is seven a factor of fifty-five. Write both answers down and ask how many divisions it took to get them.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many are standing on the shelf? Second rung, the phase's: what does anything on the shelf say about these two numbers? Third rung: the gate is cut to two small numbers that will not come out and the child reads the shelf and writes both lines. The word pad stays open.

wrong.why: six out of fifty-five is a small enough miss to feel like an accident of the numbers rather than an answer, and seven sevens sitting there in neat rows look like a success.
wrong.move: sees a small leftover and calls seven nearly a factor of fifty-five.
wrong.screen: the six are drawn on the shelf outside the rows at full strength and counted one at a time. The seven rows are counted beside them and read as forty-nine, against a tray of fifty-five. The gate then asks what would have to be true of the tray for seven to be a factor of it, and the child's verdict stays in the slot throughout.

wrong.why: the question that was asked out loud was about multiples, and an answer to the question asked feels finished.
wrong.move: writes the multiple statement and leaves the factor one unsaid, as though the division had settled one question and not two.
wrong.screen: say both opens under the shelf and writes the two statements into one frame, with the same division lit behind each of them in turn, and with the leftover still standing outside the rows above them. The statement the child did write stays exactly where it was written and the second is drawn beside it rather than over it.

phases.screen: the gate holding a division that does not come out, with the leftover showing
phases.soWhat: A remainder says the bigger number is not a multiple of the smaller, and that the smaller is not a factor of the bigger.

writeup.delight: The second phase, once both tracks are running. A number that is caught by the band is not simply coloured in: the flag on the upper track and the flag on the lower track are drawn sliding towards each other until they meet in the band, where they become one card in the shared colour, and the two steps that brought them there stay drawn behind it. Run the tracks further and it happens again, and again, with the gap between the meetings always the same length. A child who holds keep going down long enough sees the whole stage scroll through meeting after meeting, and the shared band leaves the frame as open at its right hand end as the two tracks do.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase two rings of cord lie overlapping with a number written on each and both of them empty, and the factor cards wait in a row beneath. On the second the rings have already straightened into two parallel tracks that leave the frame at the right with no end mark, each carrying a few flags, and the shared band lies along them holding nothing yet. On the third the rings are dimmed right back and the divide gate stands lit beside them with a bigger number and a smaller one already loaded. On the fourth the gate holds a division that will not come out, with the board ruled and the leftover shelf beside it empty. The running count at the top left holds the cards lifted into the shared middle against the cards there are to test, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the empty overlap, or the shared band, or the gate's mouth, or the leftover shelf, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks what these two numbers are going to have in common. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any two or three numbers in the rings, either mode, with the divide gate open beside them. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on finding what two or three numbers share, listing common multiples, settling a multiple with one division, and reading what a remainder rules out.
voiceLines: Two rings, overlapping in the middle. Something is going to end up in there.
Fill both rings. Which numbers ended up standing in the middle?
Keep both tracks running. Do they stop meeting? Could they?
Must you write both lists to find out? Try one division instead.
Something is left over. Say the two things that tells you.
Two new numbers, one to a ring. What are they going to share?
Free play. Any numbers in the rings, either mode, the gate open beside them.
Fill both lists again and lift across only what is standing in each of them.
One overlap you could count, and one that kept on catching new numbers.

observations.why: One divides every number there is, so it is in both lists whatever the two numbers are.
observations.soWhat: One is a common factor of every pair of numbers, and the overlap is never empty.
observations.observe: Something was standing in the overlap before either list had been fully read.

observations.why: Both factor lists shut at their own numbers, while both lists of multiples run on for ever and so keep meeting.
observations.soWhat: Common factors can be counted and common multiples cannot, and no greatest common multiple exists.
observations.observe: The factor overlap filled and then stopped, and the multiple band never stopped.

observations.why: Dividing the bigger number by the smaller one tests the only thing the lists were going to be searched for.
observations.soWhat: One division settles whether a bigger number is a multiple of a smaller one.
observations.observe: The gate answered without either ring being filled at all.

observations.why: The division that failed to come out is the same division that answers both questions.
observations.soWhat: A remainder says it is not a multiple and that the smaller number is not a factor, at one stroke.
observations.observe: What was left over on the shelf was written into two statements, not one.

phases.screen: two empty rings with both factor lists waiting to be filled
phases.win: the overlap holds exactly the common factors and each one divides both numbers
phases.traceback: The divide gate opens beside the rings and tests each card the child moved wrongly on both numbers; a card that divides only one goes back to its ring, a shared card left out travels into the middle, and the gate reads out the whole shared list.
ladder: Test each card in the middle. Does it go into 42 exactly, and into 70 as well?
Did every card in the middle go into 20 and into 34? Did a card that goes into both stay behind?
Which card goes into every number exactly, whatever the number is?
Divide the number in each ring by the card. Nothing left over in both means it belongs in the middle.
Keep only the cards that stand in both rings, and leave the rest where they are.

phases.screen: the rings turned into two tracks leaving the frame with no end drawn
phases.win: the band keeps catching numbers as the tracks run and no last meeting is drawn
phases.traceback: The tracks run on step by step; a number with a flag on only one track goes back up to it, each missing meeting is caught as two flags slide together into the band, and the band's list is read out; for the factor question the rings fill and their middle shuts while the band keeps catching.
ladder: Run the tracks on past 36. Look for a number with a flag above and a flag below.
Does each number in the band have a flag on the 4 track and on the 10 track?
The rings above hold the same two numbers. Could their middle keep on filling?
Take a step on each track. Do the two tracks land on the same number again?
A common multiple has a flag on the top track and on the bottom track. Look further along for the next meeting.

phases.screen: the divide gate loaded with a bigger and a smaller number and the rings dimmed
phases.win: the gate returns an exact answer and the rings stay unused beside it
phases.traceback: The gate deals the bigger number into rows of the smaller again, counting each row, and sets what is left on the shelf; if the child divided the smaller by the bigger, that board is drawn first (no full row, all of it on the shelf) and both stay written; it ends on the quotient and the remainder.
ladder: Share 112 into rows of 8. How many full rows are there, and what is left?
Count the full rows of 5 on the board, then count what sits on the shelf.
Which number is shared out, 126 or 7? Share the bigger number into rows of the smaller.
Put the bigger number into the gate and divide it by the smaller.
The quotient is the number of full rows. The remainder is whatever sits on the shelf.

phases.screen: the gate holding a division that does not come out, with the leftover showing
phases.win: the leftover stands outside the rows and both statements are written under it
phases.traceback: The gate deals the rows again, counting each, and drops the leftover onto the shelf one at a time; the quotient and remainder are written beside the shelf, then the multiple statement and the factor statement are written under it, one after the other.
ladder: A leftover settles more than the multiple question. What else does it settle?
Count the full rows of 8, then count the counters left on the shelf.
How many counters sit on the shelf? Does a leftover of any size still count?
What does anything on the shelf say about these two numbers?
With nothing on the shelf, the bigger is a multiple and the smaller is a factor.

tracks.runStep: the lowest common multiple, so meetings keep their places

onWrong.marks: Nothing is marked, nothing resets, no colour means good or bad. The child's answer stays; the pad re-opens after the traceback.
tracebacks: Phase 1: The divide gate opens beside the rings and tests each card the child moved wrongly on both numbers; a card that divides only one goes back to its ring, a shared card left out travels into the middle, and the gate reads out the whole shared list.

Phase 2: The tracks run on step by step; a number with a flag on only one track goes back up to it, each missing meeting is caught as two flags slide together into the band, and the band's list is read out; for the factor question the rings fill and their middle shuts while the band keeps catching.

Phase 3: The gate deals the bigger number into rows of the smaller again, counting each row, and sets what is left on the shelf; if the child divided the smaller by the bigger, that board is drawn first (no full row, all of it on the shelf) and both stay written; it ends on the quotient and the remainder.

Phase 4: The gate deals the rows again, counting each, and drops the leftover onto the shelf one at a time; the quotient and remainder are written beside the shelf, then the multiple statement and the factor statement are written under it, one after the other.

voice.rules: Spoken on opening, as each phase begins, on each question, on a miss and on the summary page. Every line is printed in the bubble, numbers as words, by the device's own voice (Indian English first). Muting keeps the child's place; unmuting speaks on from the word it reached. If the browser refuses speech until a tap, the first line waits behind a Tap to start cover.

guide.playsOn: none: an Udgam tool opens straight on its phase; the phase's teach lines are spoken first, and a demo phase waits for the child's own act.

palette.rule: A content colour fills countable things only and chrome never borrows one; coloured numerals and words take a deeper ink of their colour (4.5:1).

items.planQuestion: Write the factors of 42 and the factors of 70, and say which numbers turn up in both.

question.en: Write the factors of 42 and the factors of 70, and say which numbers turn up in both.

items.planQuestion: Find the common factors of 20 and 34.

question.en: Find the common factors of 20 and 34.

items.planQuestion: Why is 1 a common factor of every pair of numbers you could pick?

question.en: Tap the number on a ring to change it. Which card turns up in both lists, whatever the two numbers are?

items.planAnswer: Because 1 is a factor of every number, so it has to appear in both lists

items.planQuestion: The multiples of 4 and the multiples of 6 meet at 12, 24 and 36. Is that all of them?

question.en: The multiples of 4 and 6 meet at 12, 24 and 36. Is that all of them?

items.planAnswer: No. There are infinitely many, and 48, 60 and 72 come next

items.planQuestion: Write the first four common multiples of 4 and 10.

question.en: Write the first four common multiples of 4 and 10.
The common multiples of 4 and 10 never run out. What about the common factors of 4 and 10?

items.planQuestion: Is 112 a multiple of 8? Find out without writing either list.

question.en: Is 112 a multiple of 8? Find out without writing either list. Divide, and give the quotient and the remainder.

items.planAnswer: Yes, because 112 divided by 8 is 14 with nothing over

question.en: Is 45 a multiple of 5? Divide it, then give both numbers.

items.planAnswer: Yes, because 45 divided by 5 is 9 with nothing over

question.en: Is 126 a multiple of 7? Divide, and say how many rows there are and what is left.

items.planAnswer: Yes, because 126 divided by 7 is 18 with nothing over

items.planQuestion: Divide 74 by 9. What does the answer rule out?

question.en: Divide 74 by 9. What does the answer rule out?

items.planAnswer: That 74 is a multiple of 9, and that 9 is a factor of 74

items.planQuestion: Divide 135 by 8 and say what that rules out.

question.en: Divide 135 by 8 and say what that rules out.

items.planAnswer: 135 divided by 8 is 16 with 7 left over, so 135 is not a multiple of 8 and 8 is not a factor of 135

items.planQuestion: In the board game you throw a 4 and want to move onto 57. Divide to find out whether you may.

question.en: In the board game you throw a 4 and want to move onto 57. You may land only on a multiple of 4. Divide to find out whether you may.

items.planAnswer: No. 57 divided by 4 is 14 with 1 left over, so 57 is not a multiple of 4
